name: AWS Lambda
summary: AWS’s functions service: upload a handler, connect a trigger, and pay per request and per millisecond.
intro: A Lambda function is a handler plus settings: a runtime (or a container image), a memory size from 128 MB to 10,240 MB, and a timeout of up to 15 minutes. CPU scales with memory; at 1,769 MB a function gets the equivalent of one vCPU. Each request runs in an execution environment, a Firecracker microVM that handles one request at a time. The first request to a new environment pays a cold start (downloading code, starting the runtime and running your initialisation code); later requests reuse the warm environment, so connections and clients created outside the handler carry over.

Lambda’s strength is how it plugs into the rest of AWS. Some services push events to it (API Gateway, S3 notifications, SNS, EventBridge). For queues and streams such as SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, Lambda runs an event source mapping that polls for you, hands your function batches of records and scales the number of pollers with the backlog. Billing is per request plus GB-seconds, metered to the millisecond, with a monthly free tier of one million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds.
strengths: No servers or idle cost: quiet functions cost nothing, and scaling to thousands of parallel copies is automatic
Built-in triggers from most AWS services, including managed polling of SQS and Kinesis
Fine-grained IAM: each function gets its own execution role
Provisioned concurrency and SnapStart cut cold starts when latency matters
limits: 15-minute maximum per invocation (90 minutes only for async and queue-driven calls on Lambda Managed Instances); longer jobs need durable functions, Step Functions or ECS
Payloads are capped at 6 MB for synchronous calls (200 MB when streaming the response) and 1 MB for asynchronous ones
Default account limit of 1,000 concurrent executions per Region, shared by all functions; a spike in one can throttle the others
Cold starts range from under 100 ms to over a second, and one request per environment means many connections to your database

story: Even on EC2, reacting to something small, like a file landing in S3 or a row changing in DynamoDB, meant running a server that sat waiting for it, sized, patched and paid for around the clock. In 2013 AWS’s Tim Wagner and Jeff Barr talked about a service where developers could hand over just their code and let the cloud store and run it. Wagner wrote the PRFAQ (Amazon’s mock press release and FAQ) that proposed it.

AWS announced Lambda at re:Invent on November 13, 2014, as a preview. It ran only Node.js, could be triggered by S3, DynamoDB and Kinesis, let a function use 128 MB to 1 GB of memory for up to 60 seconds, and charged per request plus compute time in units of 100 milliseconds. It was declared ready for production on April 9, 2015, adding synchronous request/response calls and SNS as a trigger. To keep customers apart, AWS first ran functions on traditional VMs, then built Firecracker so it could scale faster without giving up that isolation.

Lambda became the reference point for what people now call “serverless”. Its limits have grown steadily (15-minute timeouts, 10 GB of memory, container images, 1 ms billing), and in 2025 durable functions let one function pause and resume across steps for up to a year.

choices.choice: Triggered by events from other AWS services
choices.why: Lambda launched as the code that runs when something changes in S3, DynamoDB or Kinesis, so nobody had to keep a server polling for it. Those integrations are still its main reason to exist.

choices.choice: Billing per request and per slice of runtime
choices.why: Charging in 100 ms units (1 ms since 2020) instead of per hour means idle code costs nothing, which is what makes small, spiky workloads cheap.

choices.choice: Virtual machines rather than shared containers
choices.why: Containers were faster and denser, but AWS chose VM-level isolation between customers from the start. When plain VMs proved too slow to scale, it built Firecracker microVMs instead of relaxing the boundary.
